xinjiang: Xinjiang is split by the Tian Shan mountain range into the Dzungarian Basin in the north and the Tarim Basin in the south. The Karakoram, Kunlun and Tian Shan ranges occupy much of its borders and its western and southern regions. Most of it is uninhabitable desert and dry grassland, and only about 9.7 per cent of the land is fit for habitation, mostly in oases at the foot of the mountains, where the cities lie. Its older English-language names include Chinese Turkestan and East Turkestan, and the Chinese called it Xiyu, the Western Regions.

Crossed by the Northern Silk Road, the Tarim and Dzungaria were known as the Western Regions. At the start of the Han dynasty the region was ruled by the Xiongnu. In the 2nd century BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian west to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi, and in 60 BCE the Han established the Protectorate of the Western Regions at Wulei. The area, once inhabited by Indo-European Tocharians and Iranian Sakas who followed Buddhism and Zoroastrianism, became Muslim in the 10th century with the conversion of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which held Kashgar.

The Uyghur state of the Turpan-Urumchi region submitted to Genghis Khan in 1209, and Xinjiang later came under Kaidu, a descendant of Ögedei Khan. In the 18th century the Qing fought the Dzungars for decades; Qing Manchu Bannermen then carried out the Dzungar genocide, nearly eradicating them and depopulating Dzungaria, and by 1759 China controlled both Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin. The two were governed separately until 1884, when the Qing established the province of Xinjiang. After the fall of the Qing in 1912, Yang Zengxin ruled it for the Republic of China until 1928. The region became part of the People's Republic of China in 1949 and an autonomous region in 1955.

Xinjiang, officially the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is the largest province-level division of China, covering more than 1.6 million square kilometres in the northwest. It is home to the Uyghurs, Han Chinese, Hui, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Mongols and other peoples, with several autonomous prefectures and counties for minorities. Its largest cities include Ürümqi, Turpan, Kashgar and Karamay, and it has substantial oil and mineral reserves.
